title: India's SIF Surge: How a New Fund Class Is Disrupting HNI Investing
excerpt: Specialized Investment Funds have amassed nearly ₹10,000 crore in six months, offering hedge-fund strategies at mutual fund prices and squeezing AIFs and PMS providers.
body:
• Specialized Investment Funds (SIFs) have surged from ₹2,010 crore in AUM at launch in October 2025 to ₹9,711 crore by February 2026, drawing capital away from Category III AIFs and PMS providers.
  • SIFs require a minimum investment of ₹10 lakh — far below the ₹50 lakh for PMS or ₹1 crore for AIFs — while offering hedge-fund-style strategies like long-short equity within a mutual fund framework.
  • During the Q1 2026 market correction, hybrid long-short SIFs fell only 3.1% on average versus a 7.8% decline in their benchmark, showcasing their downside protection potential.
  • Industry experts caution that with limited track records, investors should allocate no more than 10% of their portfolio and evaluate performance over a full market cycle.

A new class of investment vehicle is reshaping how India's wealthy invest. Specialized Investment Funds, introduced by the Securities and Exchange Board of India last year, have amassed nearly ₹10,000 crore in assets in under six months — and their rapid growth is squeezing established players in the Category III alternative investment fund and portfolio management services space.

Bridging a Long-Standing Gap

For years, Indian investors faced a stark choice: stay within the simplicity of mutual funds or leap to the ₹50 lakh minimum of PMS or the ₹1 crore threshold of AIFs. There was no middle ground. SIFs fill that gap with a minimum investment of ₹10 lakh per asset management company, offering strategies previously reserved for sophisticated institutional investors.

The framework, notified by SEBI in February 2025 and effective from April 1 of that year, allows fund managers to employ long-short equity strategies, concentrated portfolios of 15-20 stocks, derivatives overlays, sector rotation and tactical debt positioning — all within the regulated, transparent structure of a mutual fund.

"There was no middle ground. You either stayed simple or jumped straight into expensive, complex territory."

— Value Research analysis

Early Performance Under Fire

SIFs faced their first real test during the sharp Q1 2026 market correction, when the Nifty 500 fell roughly 14% as the West Asia conflict escalated and foreign investors continued selling amid high valuations. Hybrid long-short SIFs delivered an average negative return of 3.1% in the quarter, significantly outperforming their benchmark's 7.8% decline and the 8.1% average loss in traditional balanced advantage funds.

Equity-oriented SIFs posted a negative 10.1% return, compared with a 13.9% decline in the Nifty 500 total return index and 13.1% losses in flexicap mutual funds.

"Since SIFs use long-short and derivatives strategies, performance needs to be seen across at least one full market cycle," said Feroze Azeez, joint CEO of Anand Rathi Wealth Ltd. "Early NAVs are broadly around the launch price of ₹10, signalling it is too soon to judge."

Why AIFs and PMS Should Worry

SIFs are eating into a market that PMS and Category III AIF providers had to themselves. The appeal is straightforward: mutual fund-style taxation, daily or periodic liquidity, regulatory transparency, and strategies that generate returns in both bull and bear markets — all at a fraction of the entry cost.

If equity exposure exceeds 65%, SIF taxation mirrors that of an equity mutual fund. In contrast, PMS structures create a taxable event with each trade in the investor's name. Category III AIFs face their own tax complexities depending on legal structure.

The competitive pressure is accelerating. At least three new SIF launches were announced in April 2026 alone, including offerings from Franklin Templeton and Quant Mutual Fund, expanding the category beyond its initial hybrid long-short dominance into equity long-short and active asset allocation strategies.

NRI Considerations

For non-resident Indian investors managing portfolios in India, SIFs offer a compelling proposition — sophisticated strategies with lower minimum commitments and cleaner tax treatment than PMS. However, NRIs should verify whether specific SIF schemes accept non-resident investments, as SEBI compliance and FEMA regulations may apply.

What's Next

Experts recommend a cautious approach. Vishal Dhawan, co-founder of Plan Ahead Wealth Advisors, advises keeping SIF allocation below 10% of a portfolio until multi-cycle track records emerge. With seven additional strategy categories now available, the SIF landscape is poised for rapid expansion — potentially doubling AUM again before year-end.
